title: Abstraction and Interfaces
goal: Abstract classes, interfaces, default methods aur SOLID ka practical use.
objectives: Choose between an abstract class and an interface with a reason
Implement multiple interfaces in one class
Use default and static interface methods without abusing them
Explain the first SOLID principles with a code example
definition: Abstraction exposes what an object does while hiding how. An abstract class can hold state and partly implemented behaviour but cannot be instantiated. An interface declares a contract; a class can implement many interfaces, and interfaces may provide default and static methods.
explain: An abstract class is a partially built class: it can have fields, constructors and concrete methods, plus abstract methods that subclasses must implement. It expresses a shared identity with shared code. You extend one.

An interface expresses a capability — Comparable, Runnable, List. A class can implement several, which is how Java gets multiple-type behaviour without multiple inheritance. Since Java 8 interfaces can carry default methods (so old implementers do not break) and static helpers.

Program to the interface, not the implementation. A method that takes List<String> works with ArrayList, LinkedList or a test double. That is the dependency-inversion idea behind Spring injection, and it is why interfaces make code testable.
hinglish: Abstract class adhuri class hai: fields, constructor, concrete methods aur kuch abstract methods. Subclass ko extend karte ho — sirf ek. Interface capability batata hai (Runnable, Comparable), aur ek class kai interfaces implement kar sakti hai.

Interface ke against code likho, implementation ke against nahi. Method List<String> le to ArrayList, LinkedList ya test double — sab chalenge. Yahi idea Spring ki dependency injection aur testability ka base hai.
analogy: Interface ek job description hai: 'drive a car' — kis car se, ye implementation decide karti hai. Abstract class ek training program hai jisme kuch modules already complete hote hain aur kuch trainee ko khud karne hote hain.
why: Every serious Java codebase is organised around interfaces: repositories, services, listeners, comparators. Interviews ask abstract class versus interface immediately, and SOLID questions assume you can apply the answer to real code.

syntax.note: An abstract class may mix state, shared behaviour and abstract methods. It cannot be instantiated with new.
Interfaces can have abstract, default and static methods. Fields are implicitly public static final.

topics.title: Abstract classes and methods
topics.body: A class with an abstract method must be abstract; it cannot be instantiated. Subclasses either implement every abstract method or are abstract themselves. Abstract classes are ideal for a template with shared state and partial implementation.

topics.title: Interfaces
topics.body: An interface declares method signatures (and constants). Implementing classes supply the bodies. A reference typed as the interface can point at any implementation, which is the basis of substitutability and mocking.

topics.title: Multiple interface implementation
topics.body: A class can implement several interfaces, so it can be Runnable, Comparable and AutoCloseable at once. If two interfaces provide the same default method, the class must override it and can call InterfaceName.super.method().

topics.title: Default and static methods
topics.body: Default methods let an interface evolve without breaking implementers; they should be small and optional. Static interface methods are utility factories scoped to the interface.

topics.title: Functional interfaces
topics.body: An interface with exactly one abstract method is functional and can be implemented with a lambda: Runnable, Comparator, Predicate, Function. @FunctionalInterface makes the compiler enforce the single-method rule.

topics.title: Interface vs abstract class
topics.body: Use an interface for a capability shared by unrelated types, and for the API boundary. Use an abstract class when implementations share state or substantial code and belong to one family. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.

topics.title: Encapsulation, abstraction and SOLID
topics.body: Encapsulation hides data; abstraction hides implementation behind a contract. S: one reason to change. O: extend without editing. L: a subtype must honour the parent's contract. I: small interfaces. D: depend on abstractions, not concretions.

examples.title: Abstract template with shared code
lines: Report owns the title and the render format, which every report shares.
body() is abstract, so each report supplies only its own content.
SalesReport passes its title through super and implements body().
render() calls body() polymorphically, producing the final two lines.

examples.title: Two interfaces, one class
lines: Notebook implements both contracts, so it can be used wherever either type is required.
write appends to the private buffer; read exposes it.
The Readable reference only sees read(), which is enough for printing.
instanceof confirms the object also satisfies Writable at runtime.

mistakes.wrong: abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); }  Shape s = new Shape();
mistakes.why: An abstract class cannot be instantiated; the compiler rejects new Shape(). Use a concrete subclass.

mistakes.wrong: interface Repo { void save(); default void saveAll(List<Item> items) { for (Item i : items) save(); } }
mistakes.right: Keep default methods small and optional; put required behaviour in the interface contract.
mistakes.why: Default methods are for compatible evolution. Heavy logic in an interface hides dependencies and is hard to override cleanly.

debug.brief: This class does not compile because it does not honour its interface. Implement the missing method.
hints: A concrete class must implement every abstract interface method.
Add public String greet(String name) and return the text.

best: Program to interfaces in method parameters and fields.
Keep interfaces small and purpose-specific (interface segregation).
Use @FunctionalInterface when the interface is meant for a lambda.
Do not add a default method just to avoid changing implementers — fix the design instead.
tip: The abstract-class-versus-interface answer lands when you add a use case: 'a Payment abstract class for shared amount/validation, a Refundable interface because not every payment is refundable'. That shows the design reasoning interviewers listen for.
revision: Abstract class: shared state/code, one parent, cannot instantiate.
Interface: contract/capability, many implementations, default and static methods.
One abstract method = functional interface = lambda-compatible.
Depend on abstractions (D in SOLID) to keep code testable.

practice.title: Shape interface
practice.prompt: Define Shape with area() and perimeter(); implement Circle and Rectangle; print from a Shape[].
practice.hint: Only the interface type belongs in the loop variable.

practice.title: Functional greeting
practice.prompt: Create a functional interface Formatter with format(String) and implement it twice with lambdas.
practice.hint: Assign a lambda to a Formatter variable, then call format.

practice.title: Refactor to an interface
practice.prompt: Take a service class that news up a repository and refactor it to depend on a Repository interface.
practice.hint: Constructor-inject the interface; pass a fake in a test.

mcqs.q: How many classes can a Java class extend?
mcqs.explain: Java allows single class inheritance; multiple interfaces provide the rest.

mcqs.q: An interface with exactly one abstract method can be…
mcqs.explain: That is a functional interface, the target type for a lambda.

mcqs.q: Which SOLID principle says depend on abstractions?
mcqs.explain: Dependency inversion: high-level modules depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.

interview.q: Abstract class vs interface — how do you decide?
interview.a: Use an interface for a capability or API boundary shared by unrelated types, and when multiple implementations must be substitutable. Use an abstract class when implementations genuinely share state or a template algorithm. A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class.
interview.followUp: Can an abstract class have no abstract methods? (Yes, but then an interface is usually the clearer design.)

interview.q: What is the Liskov substitution principle?
interview.a: A subtype must be usable wherever the supertype is expected without breaking correctness: it must honour the parent's contract, not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions. A Square that changes Rectangle's setWidth behaviour violates it.
interview.followUp: How do you fix a Liskov violation? (Change the hierarchy — often composition instead of inheritance — rather than adding instanceof checks.)

lab.title: Payment through an interface
lab.brief: Read a payment method (upi or card) and an amount. Print '<method> paid <amount>' with two decimals.
hints: Assign the right implementation to the Payment variable.

checkpoint.title: Abstractions chosen deliberately?
checks: I can justify an interface over an abstract class with a real case
I have implemented two interfaces in one class
